draft.briefing: Hey, you're in Amboli! This little hill station sits around 700 m up in the Western Ghats, the last one before the hills drop down to the Goa coast. It gets about 7 m of rain a year, the highest in Maharashtra, so the monsoon brings mist and waterfalls everywhere.
draft.hungryLine: Do what everyone does here and grab hot kanda bhaji and vada pav from the stalls along the road between the bus stand and the police check post.

moodReplies.show-me-around: Head 5 km out to the Hiranyakeshi Temple, where a river starts from a cave, then on to Kavleshet Point for big valley views.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Find a spot with a mountain view near Sunset Point and just watch the mist roll through, Amboli is made for slow days.
moodReplies.surprise-me: Amboli started life as a staging post on the road from Vengurla port to Belgaum, which the British used to supply their garrisons in south and central India.

legends.title: The cave beside the temple
legends.body: Right next to the temple where the river begins there's a cave, and locals say you can go in and explore it. Ask around before you try, the roads out here are quiet.

tips.title: Come in June or July.
tips.body: The monsoon is the best season here, and outside it the town goes quiet and a bit deserted.

tips.title: Shout your name at Kavleshet.
tips.body: The valley throws it right back at you, and the signboards there are only in Hindi or Marathi, so keep a map handy.

story.title: Where a river is born
story.body: The Hiranyakeshi river rises in the hills around Amboli, and an ancient Shiva temple, Hiranyakeshwar, sits at the cave where the water comes out. Farmers here grow rice along it.

story.title: A stop on the supply road
story.body: Amboli came into being as a staging post on the road from Vengurla port to Belgaum. The British used that road heavily to supply their garrisons in south and central India.

story.title: The rain capital
story.body: Visitors come from Goa and Belgaum on weekends for the huge rainfall, mist and waterfalls. The Western Ghats around here are a biodiversity hotspot, though forest loss is slowly changing them.

food.detail: Near Sunset Point, with good seating and a mountain view
